Project onboarding · last updated Nov 11, 2026

Standout Camp Lantern

A camp lantern built like a tape measure. It carries in one hand. Pull the blade up and it stands as a six-foot mast of light. Send it back in and the light goes off.

Stage basic concept validated Bench test completed by Lia + TJ Next step detailed bench validation

Progress update · November 11, 2026: Lia and TJ have completed a basic bench test validating the idea, as confirmed by Max. The detailed mast, coil-fatigue and electronics tests, dimensions and performance targets in this presentation remain to be verified; this is not a completed product validation.

The idea

Camp light works best from overhead. A lantern usually ends up on the ground or the table, where it shines in your eyes and leaves everything past the table dark. Getting it higher takes a branch, a pole or a headlamp. This lantern carries its own pole: a steel tape blade with a light strip along it.

Packs small

Blade, battery and electronics wind into a housing about 4.5 in square. Three wire legs fold flat against the body.

Stands tall

The blade pulls out to any height up to 6 ft and stays there. The light comes on along the blade as it leaves the housing.

Puts itself away

Press the release and a spring winds the blade back in, the light going out as it goes. This is the part that should feel magical.

Standout Camp Lantern is the development name. Standout is the tape-measure term for how far a blade extends before it buckles.

Four ways to use it

The design and the tests target the vertical mast. The reach and the span come free with the tape-measure form and are not rated. The lantern uses an accessory diffuser bag, which test 1 checks separately because the bag adds weight at the tip and catches wind.

How it works

Three ideas carry the design.

1. The blade is the pole

A tape-measure blade is curved across its width. Pulled out, the curve makes it stiff enough to stand on its own. Pressed flat, it winds onto a reel. The LED strip is bonded along the outside of that curve under a thin frosted skin, so the whole lit length coils up with the blade.

Cross-section with the lit face up and thickness exaggerated. The strip sits on the outside of the coil, so winding stretches it. The total must stay near 2.0 mm.

2. Everything rides in the reel

The battery sits crosswise inside the reel hub, with the driver board, button and USB-C port beside it. All of it turns with the reel, so the strip is wired straight to the board and nothing electrical has to cross a rotating joint.

Housing is 114.3 mm square. The coil leaves about 2 mm of clearance per side and the cell leaves under 1 mm per end, so both depend on the 2.0 mm laminate.

3. The light follows the blade

Two small magnetic sensors count reel turns, the controller converts turns into length, and only the strip segments that are clear of the housing are switched on. Pulling the blade is the on switch. Try it:

Blade out 3 ft 4 inSegments lit 0 of 22Reel turns 0Sensor count 0

Segments are drawn at 83 mm, the pitch of the 24 V white strip. A segment switches on only once it is fully past the mouth.

More drawings · reel cross-section, exit path, electronics, sensing, lock and damper

Reel cross-section, to scale

The housing is 50.8 mm wide: 2.5 mm walls, 1.5 mm flanges, a 33 mm blade channel and 8.5 mm reserved for the spring.

Exit path

The blade goes from flat to fully curved in about 57 mm, and the strip has to follow it on every pull.

Electronics

Everything here rides in the rotating hub; only the three strip pads leave it. The strip rail is switched off whenever the blade is home. Its voltage depends on which strip wins the bench tests.

Turn sensing

A third, always-on low-power sensor wakes the controller when the blade first moves.

Lock and damper (prototype 2)

What has to be proven

The design fits on paper, with little room to spare. Three questions decide whether it works in practice. Each has a cheap bench test that answers it before any housing is made.

Does it stand?

The blade has to hold a strip and its skin 6 ft up, through a lean and a breeze. Test 1 finds the blade and strip widths that do.

Does the strip survive the coil?

The strip winds into about 6.5 tight turns and has to come back out working, hundreds of times. The laminate must also stay near 2.0 mm thick or the coil outgrows the housing. Test 2 is the make-or-break one.

Does the light keep up?

The controller has to track the blade without losing count, and one cell has to run the strip for about two hours. Test 3 checks both.

The plan

Nothing is built at full size until the bench tests have fixed the blade, strip, reel and battery.

Bench tests

Three tests, in this order of importance. Tests 1 and 3 can start together; test 2 uses the winning samples from test 1.

Test 1: mast · how tall does the loaded blade stand?

Picks the blade width, strip width, skin weight budget and throat length.

Setup. Cut 6.5 ft of blade per sample: 6 ft of mast plus 6 in held in a printed throat block clamped to the bench edge, slot pointing up. Bond each strip to the outside face with transfer tape, centered on the crown. Weigh and measure every sample first.

SampleBladeStrip
A32 mmNone (baseline)
B32 mmWide
C32 mm5 mm
D25 mmWide
E25 mm5 mm
  1. Still air. Extend to 4, 5 and 6 ft with the 25 mm throat. Hold each for 60 seconds.
  2. Lean. Tilt the block off vertical in 5° steps until the blade buckles: toward the lit face, away from it, and sideways.
  3. Wind. Desk fan on low and high, face-on and edge-on, at each height.
  4. Added weight. Add vinyl tape to simulate the skin at +10, +20 and +30 g/m and repeat at 6 ft.
  5. Throat length. Repeat the 6 ft lean test with 15 mm and 40 mm throats.
  6. Horizontal reference. Extend each sample horizontally, lit face up then down, and note where it buckles.
  7. Diffuser bag. Sew or tape a 24 in and a 72 in bag in each fabric and weigh them. Hook each to the tip of the best sample and repeat the still-air, lean and fan steps at the bag's height. With a strip lit, compare brightness at 1 m with and without the bag using a phone light-meter app.

Record. Laminate thickness at three points, weight per meter, height reached, buckling angle each way, fan result.

Pass (proposed). Stands at 6 ft for 60 seconds, survives a 10° lean in every direction and the fan on high face-on, all with a throat of 25 mm or shorter. If nothing passes at 6 ft, rate the product at 5 ft and rerun.

Bag pass (proposed). With the 24 in bag: stands for 60 seconds, survives a 10° lean and the fan on low. With the 72 in bag: record what it survives; it is expected to need still air. The bag should pass at least half the light.

Test 2: coil fatigue · does the bonded strip survive winding?

The make-or-break test. Fixes the hub diameter, the real coil size and therefore the battery.

Why two hubs. The product has one hub. The 76 mm hub is the design size, because it is the smallest a 21700 cell fits inside crosswise. The 60 mm hub is a deliberate stress case: it bends the strip about 27% tighter, so passing on it shows the design has margin.

Setup. Print both hubs with flanges 33 mm apart, a slot to anchor the blade end and a hand crank. Mount each on a stand with a throat block about 57 mm from the coil. Build 6 ft samples from the best pairings in test 1, one with no skin and one with the silicone skin. Wire each strip to the bench supply so every segment can be lit.

  1. Wind fully, pull fully out: one cycle.
  2. Every 50 cycles, inspect: every segment lights with no flicker when flexed; no lifting at strip edges or ends; no kinks; blade springs back to its full curve (measure crown depth at three points); coil diameter when wound; turns not sliding sideways.
  3. Run every sample to 500 cycles on both hubs, then the best one to 2,000. A slow cordless drill on the crank saves time.
  4. Dwell. Leave one sample fully wound for 48 hours somewhere warm, then check it.
  5. Cold. Freeze one wound sample for 2 hours, then cycle it 20 times right away.

Also record the blade length paid out at each full turn. The controller needs this as its turns-to-length table.

Pass (proposed). 500 cycles with no dead segments and no lifting beyond the last few millimeters; crown depth within 10% after the dwell; wound coil no larger than 105 mm on the 76 mm hub.

ResultDecision
Passes on 76 mm, coil 105 mm or less76 mm hub, single 21700 cell
Passes only on 76 mm, coil too largeThinner strip or skin, or drop to 5 ft
Passes on 60 mm as wellOption to shrink the housing or thicken the skin, with a pouch battery
Fails on bothSwitch to a strip that floats in a sleeve, and retest
Test 3: electronics · does the light follow the blade?

Runs on a breadboard in two parts. The control part runs from the bench supply now; the battery part waits until the strip and its voltage are chosen.

Control part. Wire the controller to the strip through the level shifter. Fit eight magnets with alternating poles around the flange of the 76 mm test hub and fix the sensors beside it, a quarter-step apart.

  • Counts up and down correctly with no missed counts when the hub is spun fast.
  • Turns convert to blade length using the table from test 2.
  • Only segments past the throat are lit.
  • Light comes on when the first segment clears the throat and goes off at home.
  • The strip rail is switched off whenever the blade is home.
  • A tap steps through three brightness levels; a hold turns the light off.

Battery part. Add the cell, protection board, charger and boost converter.

MeasureTarget (proposed)
Runtime at each brightness levelAt least 2 hours at full
Standby current with the blade homeUnder 50 µA
Voltage at the far end of the strip, full brightnessWithin 0.5 V of the near end
Cell temperature after 30 minutes at fullUnder 45 °C
Flicker, checked with a phone camera in slow motionNone visible
Plugging in the charger with the blade homeResets the turn count
Low batterySteps down, then shuts off before the cell protection trips

Prototypes

Prototype 1a: bench-powered · final size, hand rewind, power through a cable

Proves the packaging, the mast and the light following the blade, without committing to a battery or strip voltage.

  • Cable. A flexible three-core cable (power, ground, data) enters on the hub axis, through the hole where the button will later sit, and joins the strip leads inside the hub.
  • Twist. It twists about 6.5 turns as the blade pulls out and untwists on rewind. Leave about 1 m hanging free and clamp it at the hub face so the solder joints carry no load.
  • Controller. On the bench at the far end of the cable. Keep the cable under about 2 m; long data runs can glitch.
  • Sensing. Sensors fixed in the housing wall, magnets on the hub flange, so their wires do not rotate.
  • Dummy weight. About 70 g in the cell cradle so the base balances as the finished unit will.

Printed parts. Housing in two halves split on the reel plane with drain holes; hub with flanges, cell cradle and blade anchor; hub face cap with a knurled rim as the rewind wheel; replaceable throat insert; blade tip cap with a pull ring that the bag hooks onto; three wire tripod legs with their recesses, pivot posts and channel; blank cover for the spring bay.

It must show

  • The reel, coil and throat fit in 114.3 × 114.3 × 50.8 mm with the spring bay left empty.
  • The mast stands at the rated height on a table, on grass and on uneven ground.
  • The base does not tip in a light breeze with the tripod legs out.
  • Light follows the blade in both directions, with nothing lit inside the housing.
  • 50 extend-and-rewind cycles by hand without a jam or a broken cable lead.
  • With the unit inside the bag, 20 pulls and rewinds by the tip ring without fabric snagging in the mouth.
Prototype 1b: self-contained · battery and electronics move into the hub

Once the strip and its voltage are fixed, the cell, protection board, charger, boost converter, controller and sensors move into the hub. The magnets move to the housing wall, and the USB-C port and button take over the hub face.

  • The cell and driver electronics fit the 72 mm bore.
  • Charging through the hub-face port works at any hub angle.
  • Runtime at full brightness matches the bench measurement.
  • One evening of real use outdoors, including dew, with the unit still working the next day.
Prototype 2: auto-retract · the part that should feel magical
  • Spring. A power spring about 8 mm wide in the bay beside the reel, salvaged from a donor tape measure to start.
  • Lock. A pawl engages ratchet teeth on the flange rim, so the mast holds at any height by default. A button on the housing releases it.
  • Damper. A small rotary damper geared to the flange limits the rewind speed.
  • Tip. A soft tip cap absorbs the last impact at the mouth.
TuneTarget (proposed)
Pull-out forceComfortable with one hand, roughly 5–10 N
Full retraction from 6 ft2–3 seconds
Arrival at the mouthNo slap, no bounce
HoldMast stays put at any height with the button released

Prove. 1,000 spring retractions with no dead segments and no jam; full retraction when cold and with a wet, gritty blade; turn count still correct after fast retractions.

Risks and open questions

The two risks that could sink the concept are strip survival in the coil and laminate thickness. Test 2 retires both.

RiskRetired byFallback
Strip cracks from repeated coilingTest 2Strip floating in a sleeve; larger hub with a pouch battery
Laminate thicker than 2.0 mm, so the coil outgrows the housingCalipers, then test 2Pouch battery on a smaller hub; 5 ft blade
Mast buckles in wind or on a leanTest 1Rate at 5 ft; longer throat; prop or guy point
Coil slides sideways on the strip ridgeTest 2Closer-fitting flanges; a wider strip
Blade loses its curve when stored woundTest 2 dwellDifferent blade stock; storage temperature limit
Turn count drifts, wrong segments litTest 3Re-zero on charge; dedicated home sensor
Steel blade shorts or carries static to the circuitTest 3Coated blade stock; ground through a resistor
Water and grit in the reelPrototype 1 outdoorsWiper, drains, sealed hub
Base tips with the mast upPrototype 1Longer legs; a stake or guy lines
Spring and battery compete for widthPrototype 2A 25 mm blade frees 7 mm
Diffuser bag acts as a sail and pulls the mast overTest 1, bag stepShorter bag; vented top; guy loops on the bag
Bag fabric snags in the mouth on rewindPrototype 1aStandoff ring at the tip; stiffer hem at the bag top
  • Which strip wins: 24 V white at 10 mm wide, or 5 V color-mixing at 5 mm? Thickness and tests 1 and 2 decide.
  • Is the donor blade's coating enough insulation under the strip, or does it need a film layer?
  • Should the release button sit on the housing, or is a twist of the hub face a better gesture?
  • What is the target retail price? It bounds the cell, strip and board choices.
  • Body thickness: 59 mm with the 32 mm blade centered, as in the 3D model, or 50.8 mm with a 25 mm blade?
  • How does the bag top attach to the tip: a hook on the ring, a pocket, or a magnet? And is the bag sold with the light or as an add-on?

Five orders, one per phase, so nothing is bought before the phase that needs it. Picks were checked on the maker's or seller's own page on Nov 10, 2026, except where marked not verified.
